From what I remember, there are three different alphabets, two of which are nearly identical in use but have no relation in appearances.

Hiragana has more curves, and is used for Japanese specific things. 46 basic letters, with 68 alternate versions (Ga is an alternate version of Ka, with a simple ' to mark the difference).

Katakana has more angles, and is used for non-Japanese things, and names. Same exact system as Hiragana, but replacing all of the original 46 with other symbols.

Kanji is seperate from the other two, using single symbols to represent entire words (your full mailing address can be put into a single Kanji), but the systems each Kanji is based off of might be hard to keep track of.
So, which do you think would be better to learn first? Katakana, Hiragana, or Kanji? Or start with speaking the language over reading/writing it?

Start with Hiragana. It's been a while, but I'm almost positive that all pieces of grammar specific words (like And, Or, You, Me, They, it) are in hiragana writing, as are many nouns and verbs.

The language is very easy to learn how to speak.

"a" (like in Ka, Ha, or Ma) is pronounced like ah, hah, or Pa. The Japanese letter "Pa" sounds just like how we would say Pa.

"i" sounds like feet, tweet, screech. The letter "Mi" sounds like Me.

"u" is like woo, true, sue. The letter "Bu" sounds like Boo.

"e" is always pronounced like eh, get, pet. The letter "He" sounds like Heh.

"o" is always like oh, mope, slope. The letter "Do" sounds like Dough.

The only common exception is the letter "Su", which almost always has the vowel being silent. For example, the name "Sosuke" is often pronounced Sohs-Kay, not Soh-Soo-Kay. Whether or not this is caused from natural slang or is a part of the grammar is beyond me. It's been a long time since I studied Japanese (about 8 years), so you might have better luck asking someone else.

Do you find that there are any table manners that are outdated/unnecessary? The elbows on the table one is not a big rule in my house because I've heard it's a carryover from sailors using their elbows to steady their food. Navy recruiters would try to identify people with prior sailing experience, so sailors would remind each other to keep their elbows off of the table to avoid standing out. I'm not sure if the story is true, but it does seem like a table rule that we keep alive mainly for the tradition of it.

here is an excellent article about table manners, how they've changed but the premise is still the same http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2011/nov/09/history-table-manners-etiquette-beeton

Elbows on the table, for me is about a step away from the 'prison stance' where you have one hand with a utensil guarding your plate, and the other hooked around the other side and holding on for dear life to your purple drink. I also don't abide by the hand under the table, if the forearms are resting on the edge, that's good

Nope, you're stuck with it. If it makes you feel better, as much as 90% of the population has it, even if they don't exhibit symptoms.

"Genital herpes is a chronic, life-long viral infection. Two types of HSV can cause genital herpes: HSV-1 and HSV-2. Most cases of recurrent genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, and approximately 50 million persons in the United States are infected with this type of genital herpes (318). However, an increasing proportion of anogenital herpetic infections have been attributed to HSV-1 infection, which is especially prominent among young women and MSM (319-321)."

Source: http://www.cdc.gov/std/tg2015/herpes.htm

Basically there is no cure. The remedy is to keep one's immune system strong in order to prevent viral outbreaks.

The most common causes of a weak immune system are: sugar, smoking, junk food, wheat, sunburn, over-work, stress, and many pharmaceuticals.
